turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning. I'll grab a blood pressure before Doctor Hale sees you. Right arm out, thanks.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm. Yeah. Thing always pinches. I don't know.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Hold still. Right. One hundred and fifty eight over ninety two. Pulse seventy six.
[SEG0004] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): That can't be right. At home this morning it was one thirty four over eighty. I put it in the book.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): This is the clinic reading, one fifty eight on ninety two. And the bottle in your bag says amlodopine ten milligram.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Ten? I take twenty milligram of that. Err. I don't know.
[SEG0007] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The box says ten. He keeps saying twenty.
[SEG0008] person_4 (DOCTOR): G'day. I'm Doctor Hale, sorry about the wait. What's brought you in?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): It's me ankles, they're puffed up. And I'm on the loo all the time. I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0010] person_4 (DOCTOR): Swollen ankles, and passing urine a lot. How long have the ankles been swollen?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Err. Two weeks, I reckon. I don't know.
[SEG0012] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Three weeks, easy. Since the long weekend he's had his shoes off.
[SEG0013] person_4 (DOCTOR): You don't agree, so I'll put roughly two to three weeks, nothing firmer. Is it both ankles?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, both. Worse of an arvo.
[SEG0015] person_4 (DOCTOR): And the passing urine, daytime or night?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Night mostly. Three or four times I get up. Daytime's alright. Might be that tablet.
[SEG0017] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0019] person_4 (DOCTOR): Are you short of breath around the house?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Nah. I'm not.
[SEG0021] person_4 (DOCTOR): What about the tummy and the bowels, any trouble there?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm. No, they're fine.
[SEG0023] person_4 (DOCTOR): Let's sort the tablets. Bottle says amlodopine ten milligrams, you said twenty. What else do you take?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Frusimide, the water tablet, forty milligram every morning for the pressure. Omprazole twenty milligram for the heartburn. The amlodopine dose, I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0025] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Frusimide is every morning, forty milligrams, that's right. I've only ever seen the ten milligram amlodopine.
[SEG0026] person_4 (DOCTOR): So that's frusimide forty milligrams each morning, omprazole twenty milligrams, and amlodopine either ten or twenty. How long have you had the high blood pressure?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Five-ish years. I don't know exactly.
[SEG0028] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't think so. I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0030] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He hasn't got any. Penicillin was fine for the tooth.
[SEG0031] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll record no known allergies. Ankles are pitting, both sides. Calves soft, no tenderness. Chest is clear, no crackles.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Of.

[SEG0033] person_4 (DOCTOR): I think the ankle swelling is from the amlodopine. The getting up at night fits the water tablet. I can't rule out a heart cause altogether, but you're not breathless and the chest is clear.

[SEG0034] person_4 (DOCTOR): Here's the change. Stop the amlodopine from today. I'll start perindopril four milligrams by mouth each morning for the blood pressure. Stay on frusimide forty milligrams in the morning, and keep the omprazole as it is.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm. Perindopril. I won't remember it. Right.
[SEG0036] person_4 (DOCTOR): The chemist puts the name on the box. The nurse takes bloods Thursday morning, a kidney check. Don't fast. Take the frusimide after the bloods, not before.

[SEG0037] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll see you in two weeks. If those bloods are borderline we do a urine protein test. If the swelling does not settle by then, we book a scan of the legs. Bring the home readings, and if you feel dizzy on the new tablet, stop it and ring the clinic.
[SEG0038] person_1 (NURSE): I'll book those bloods for Thursday morning. No worries.

spec.situation: Patient on amlodipine and a water tablet with swollen ankles and passing urine often; blood pressure read at clinic and at home with different numbers; doctor changes one medicine.

traps.happens: In the plan the doctor books some tests or visits for a definite time ('the nurse takes bloods Thursday morning', 'I'll see you in two weeks') and makes others conditional ('if those are borderline we do the third test', 'if it does not settle, a scan').
traps.label_rule: Booked or arranged = status planned. Only the hedged ones are conditional. Never mark a booked test conditional or 'if needed'. Instructions for the booked test (fasting, time, medicine timing) belong to that test's action, not a separate invented plan item.

traps.happens: The transcript looks like speech-to-text: drug names are sometimes spelled wrongly ('Omprazole', 'Mizartan' for telmisartan, 'Metformine'), fragments and fillers appear ('Err', 'Of.', 'Mm.', 'Umm'), numbers are sometimes digits and sometimes words.
traps.label_rule: Medicine names are recorded as written in the transcript (name) with a normalized/generic name ONLY when the true drug is certain from context (a drug 'for the pressure' written 'Mizartan' is NOT certain enough: leave generic_name empty). Fragments and fillers are never facts.

features: spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.
disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.

bad.reason: Hypertension for about five years is supported, but reported_by was patient, not doctor.
Action supported, but responsible_person is nurse; doctor gave the instructions.
bad.text: Kidney blood test Thursday morning, no fasting, frusimide after the test (action_type=investigation, status=planned, responsible_person=nurse, time_reference=value: Thursday morning)

bad.reason: Dose disagreement supported, but family member and nurse don't explicitly state the nurse's own dose claim.
bad.text: The nurse and family member say the amlodipine dose is 10 mg while the patient says 20 mg. (type=medication_discrepancy, related_entities=medications[0], resolution_status=unresolved)

omissions.text: Amlodipine current dose was uncertain/disputed before stopping: bottle/box and family member indicated 10 mg, while patient stated 20 mg; doctor documented it as either 10 or 20 mg.
No calf swelling/mass concern on exam was supported by 'calves soft' bilaterally, in addition to no tenderness.
Doctor specifically recorded no known drug allergies after discussion ('I'll record no known allergies').
